questions.question: A student observes pollen grains dancing randomly under a microscope when suspended in water. If the water is replaced by a slightly thicker liquid at the same temperature, what is the best explanation of what happens to this motion?
options: The motion stops completely because the water molecules have disappeared.
The motion continues but becomes slower because the thicker liquid's particles collide with the pollen differently.
The motion accelerates because thicker liquids contain more energetic particles.
The pollen grains dissolve completely, meaning no motion can be observed.

questions.question: If a drop of blue food dye is carefully placed at the bottom of a still beaker of water, it slowly spreads out without being stirred. Which statement best describes the final state of the mixture?
options: The dye particles will eventually settle back at the bottom due to gravity.
The dye particles will eventually achieve a completely uniform, random distribution throughout the water.
The dye particles will cluster in the middle where there is less water pressure.
The dye particles will only spread if the water is heated to its boiling point.

questions.question: In an experiment, a student adds a drop of ink to hot water and another drop to cold water. The ink spreads much faster in the hot water. Why does this happen?
options: The particles in the hot water move more quickly, colliding with and dispersing the ink faster.
Hot water particles are larger, which pushes the ink particles further apart.
The hot water has less gravity acting on it, allowing the ink to rise.
The cold water particles have stopped moving entirely, blocking the ink.

questions.question: A student mixes a spoonful of flour into water and stirs it. Initially, the liquid looks cloudy. After leaving it on the desk for an hour, they notice a layer of flour at the bottom and clear water above. What does this tell us about the mixture?
options: It is a solution, because the flour has completely dissolved into the water.
It is a suspension, because the solid particles were visible and eventually settled over time.
It is a pure substance, because the flour and water have chemically combined.
It is a solution, because the particles have reached a permanent random distribution.

questions.question: Why does a solid lump of sugar not dissolve instantly the moment it touches water?
options: The water molecules must first freeze the sugar to break it apart.
The forces of attraction holding the sugar particles together must be overcome by interactions with the water.
The sugar particles are too heavy to be moved by the lightweight water molecules.
The sugar must melt into a liquid before it can mix with any solvent.

questions.question: A student measures 50 cm³ of ethanol and 50 cm³ of water. When they mix them together in a measuring cylinder, the total volume is recorded as 97 cm³ instead of 100 cm³. What is the most scientifically accurate explanation for this observation?
options: Some of the liquid particles evaporated instantly due to a chemical reaction.
One type of particle is smaller and fits into the spaces between the other type of particle.
The measuring cylinder shrunk when the two liquids were mixed together.
Mass was lost during the physical mixing process, reducing the volume.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios describes a key difference between the process of melting and the process of dissolving?
options: Melting requires only heat to change state, whereas dissolving requires interaction with a solvent.
Melting is a chemical change that creates new substances, while dissolving is a physical change.
Dissolving requires heat to break chemical bonds, while melting can happen at any temperature without energy.
Melting only happens to pure substances, whereas dissolving only happens to mixtures.

questions.question: A student dissolves 15 g of salt into 100 g of water in a sealed flask. What will be the total mass of the resulting salt solution?
options: Exactly 115 g, because the masses of the mixed substances add together and mass is conserved.
Slightly less than 115 g, because the salt particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
Slightly more than 115 g, because the salt particles react and gain mass from the air.
Exactly 100 g, because the dissolved salt no longer has any measurable mass.

questions.question: A student wants to measure exactly 12.5 cm³ of acid for a titration where precision is critical. Why should they choose a burette instead of a beaker?
options: A beaker is designed for heating liquids, so it cannot hold acid safely.
A burette is designed for precise volume delivery, and using the wrong equipment impacts the quality of results.
A beaker cannot hold volumes of liquid that are not whole numbers.
A burette chemically reacts with the acid to make it easier to see.

questions.question: A chemist heats a clear liquid and observes that it begins to boil at exactly 100°C, and the temperature remains constant at 100°C until all of it has boiled away. What does this tell them about the liquid?
options: The liquid is a mixture because it boiled at a single temperature.
The liquid is a pure material because it has a fixed boiling point.
The liquid is an unstable compound that is decomposing.
The liquid must be a solution of salt and water.

questions.question: Road grit (salt) is spread on icy roads in winter. How does this help clear the ice, based on physical properties?
options: The salt acts as a blanket, keeping the ice warm so it melts.
The salt acts as an impurity, lowering the melting point of the water so it melts at a lower temperature.
The salt reacts chemically with the ice, releasing heat that melts it.
The salt absorbs the water, turning the ice directly into a gas.

questions.question: A sample of wax is heated slowly, and its temperature is recorded. The wax begins to melt at 45°C, but does not completely turn into a liquid until the temperature reaches 52°C. What does this indicate about the wax?
options: The wax is a pure material that has a high heat capacity.
The wax is a mixture, which causes it to melt over a range of temperatures.
The thermometer being used is faulty and cannot read a fixed temperature.
The wax is undergoing a chemical decomposition rather than melting.

questions.question: A student keeps adding spoonfuls of sugar to 100 ml of water at room temperature. After 5 spoonfuls, no more sugar dissolves, even after stirring for 10 minutes. Why did the sugar stop dissolving?
options: The sugar molecules have bonded with each other to form an indestructible solid.
At a given temperature, there is a limit to how much solute can dissolve in a solvent.
The water molecules have evaporated, leaving no room for the sugar.
The student did not stir fast enough to break the water's chemical bonds.

questions.question: A hot, saturated solution of copper sulfate is left on a windowsill to cool down. After several hours, blue crystals are seen at the bottom of the beaker. What process explains this?
options: The copper sulfate reacted with the glass beaker to form a new compound.
As the solution cooled, the solute became less soluble and crystallized out.
The solvent expanded, pushing the solute out of the solution.
The cooling process melted the copper sulfate, turning it back into a solid.

questions.question: After plotting points for solubility versus temperature on a scatter graph, a student draws a smooth curve that passes close to most of the points. What is the primary purpose of drawing this line of best fit?
options: To connect every single data point directly to show experimental errors.
To help identify and describe the overall relationship between the two variables.
To change the actual experimental values to make the data look perfect.
To show that the independent variable did not affect the dependent variable.

questions.question: A student investigates how the temperature of water affects the solubility of salt. Which of the following is the most complete and scientifically sound conclusion for this investigation?
options: 'The temperature of the water increased as I heated it with the Bunsen burner.'
'As the temperature of the water (independent variable) increased, the amount of salt that dissolved (dependent variable) also increased.'
'Salt dissolves very well in water because water is a good solvent.'
'The amount of salt dissolved stayed at 35 grams because we used a balance to measure it.'

questions.question: A student wants to dissolve a tablet of medicine as quickly as possible. Based on scientific principles, which combination of changes would most likely increase the rate and amount of dissolving?
options: Crush the tablet into a powder and use hot water instead of cold water.
Keep the tablet whole and use cold oil instead of warm water.
Crush the tablet and use a smaller volume of cold water.
Keep the tablet whole and stir it very slowly in a saturated solution.

questions.question: In an experiment to find out how the type of solvent affects how much sugar can dissolve, a student uses water, ethanol, and propanol. What is the independent variable in this investigation?
options: The mass of sugar that dissolves.
The type of solvent used.
The temperature of the room.
The volume of solvent used.

questions.question: A student measures how long it takes for 5 grams of salt to dissolve in water at different temperatures. What is the dependent variable in this investigation?
options: The temperature of the water.
The time taken for the salt to dissolve.
The mass of the salt used.
The volume of the water.

questions.question: A student wants to test if stirring speed affects how fast sugar dissolves. They set up two beakers: Beaker A has 100 ml of hot water and is stirred quickly; Beaker B has 50 ml of cold water and is stirred slowly. Why is this not a fair test?
options: Because they used two different beakers which made the measurement of time impossible.
Because they changed multiple variables (temperature, volume, and stirring speed) instead of only changing the stirring speed.
Because stirring speed cannot be measured with standard school laboratory equipment.
Because sugar dissolves at the same rate regardless of temperature or volume.
